uses.text: About 90 % of the sulfur used in the U.S. is used as sulfuric acid.
Sulfuric acid turns phosphate rock into fertiliser and fills lead-acid batteries.
Sulfur vulcanises rubber and is used as a fungicide.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.100, massive_stars 0.613, white_dwarfs 0.288); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 81 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '29% of S ... come from SNe Ia' (figure reading 0.288). Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

bonding.note: Crowns of eight atoms, S₈, in the common yellow forms; many other rings and chains exist.

air.text: Stable in air at room temperature; burns with a blue flame to sulfur dioxide when lit.

water.text: Insoluble in water and does not react with it.

acids.text: Not attacked by non-oxidising acids; hot concentrated nitric or sulfuric acid oxidise it.

plantRole.text: Taken up as sulfate; part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine, of glutathione, and of defence compounds such as glucosinolates.

humanRole.text: Part of the amino acids methionine and cysteine; obtained from dietary protein.

roles.text: Part of the amino acids methionine and cysteine, which the rumen microbes of cattle and sheep build from the sulfur in their feed.
Part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
Part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
Part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine; one of the six elements found essential in every prokaryote analysed.

uptake.text: Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) from the soil water; leaves can also take in sulfur dioxide (SO₂) from the air

known.text: One of the ten elements recognised as essential in the second half of the 19th century, once plants could be grown in nutrient solutions

deficiency.text: Leaves lose chlorophyll and protein and the plant grows slowly. Unlike nitrogen shortage, the yellowing in wheat is spread over old and young leaves alike; in legumes, sulfur shortage looks just like nitrogen shortage.

In oilseed rape the young leaves show it first, turning reddish with dying edges, and the yellow flowers can turn white; fully developed rape leaves with less than about 6 mg of sulfur per gram of dry matter point to a shortage.

toxicity.text: Plants put up with a lot of sulfate in the soil; only very salty soils do harm. Sulfur dioxide in polluted air is more dangerous, and trees and other perennials are hurt at about half the level that harms annual plants.

soil.text: Most of a soil's sulfur is bound in organic matter, usually 100–1000 mg per kg in humid regions; it becomes available as microbes break that matter down, and sulfate is easily washed out.

Sulfur dioxide from industry once supplied much of crops' sulfur. Since emissions were cut in recent decades, sulfur shortage has become common on farmland, above all in rainy regions and on leached soils, and sulfur fertilisers are now used to correct it.

partners.text: Nitrogen fixation in legume nodules is very sensitive to sulfur shortage: early on, it suffers more than photosynthesis does.

forest.text: Sulfur rarely limits forests; trees take sulfate from the soil and some sulfur dioxide from the air.

food.text: Wheat short of sulfur makes flour whose dough stretches less and gives a smaller loaf, because its grain proteins hold less of the sulfur amino acids that link the gluten together.

The sharp taste of cabbage, mustard and their relatives comes from sulfur compounds (glucosinolates), which rise with the sulfur supply; more makes vegetables spicier but fodder less welcome to animals.

isotopeUses.text: Sulfur-35 marked the protein coat in Hershey and Chase's 1952 phage experiment; it stayed outside the infected bacteria while the DNA, labelled with phosphorus-32, went in.

history.nameOrigin: From the Latin sulfur (also spelled sulphur), the Romans' name for the substance.
history.note: Known since prehistory as brimstone. Jefferson Lab credits Lavoisier with persuading chemists around 1777 that it is an element; CIAAW credits Gay-Lussac and Thénard with proving it in 1809.

prose.text: Sulfur is a bright-yellow nonmetal, the 'brimstone' of old texts, found around volcanic vents and in large underground deposits; it is an essential part of proteins and of the sharp garlic and mustard compounds that plants make to defend themselves. Pure sulfur hardly smells; the rotten-egg odour belongs to hydrogen sulfide. Melted, it is a runny yellow liquid, but heated further it suddenly turns dark red and as thick as treacle, because its eight-atom rings break open and link into long chains. The atom, [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ (ground term ³P₂), has two unpaired 3p electrons, and nature provides four stable isotopes, mostly sulfur-32.
